chapterTag.category: AP Calc AB Unit 4 — Contextual Applications

body.en: Derivatives model the real world: velocity and acceleration, related rates, and local linear approximation.

For motion, \( v(t)=s'(t) \) and \( a(t)=v'(t) \). Related rates differentiate a relationship with respect to time. Linearization: \( L(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a) \). L'Hôpital's rule resolves \( \tfrac00 \) and \( \tfrac{\infty}{\infty} \).

caption.en: Velocity $v(t) = 3t(t-4)$ and acceleration $a(t) = 6(t-2)$. On $(2,4)$, both $v(t) < 0$ and $a(t) > 0$ (opposite signs), so speed is decreasing; on $(4,\infty)$, both are positive, so speed is increasing.

body.en:
A particle has position \( s(t)=t^{3}-6t^{2} \). When is it at rest?

\[ v(t)=3t^{2}-12t=3t(t-4)=0\ \Rightarrow\ t=0,\ 4. \]

A spherical balloon is inflated so its volume increases at 10 cm³/s. How fast is the radius increasing when \(r=5\) cm?

\[V=\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{dV}{dt}=4\pi r^2\frac{dr}{dt}.\]\[10=4\pi(25)\frac{dr}{dt}\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{dr}{dt}=\frac{10}{100\pi}=\frac{1}{10\pi}\approx0.032\text{ cm/s}.\]

label.en: ⚠ Common traps — Speeding up vs slowing down & early substitution

body.en:
Speeding up requires matching signs: A particle is speeding up when velocity \( v(t) \) and acceleration \( a(t) \) have the same sign (both positive or both negative). It is slowing down when they have opposite signs. A negative acceleration does NOT automatically mean slowing down!

Premature variable substitution in related rates: Never plug changing numeric quantities (e.g. \( r = 5 \) or \( h = 4 \)) into your geometric formula before differentiating! Differentiate the equation implicitly with respect to \( t \) first, then substitute instantaneous values.

Displacement vs total distance: Displacement over \( [a, b] \) is \( \int_a^b v(t)\,dt = s(b) - s(a) \). Total distance travelled requires integrating speed: \( \int_a^b |v(t)|\,dt \).

solution.en: Form \(0/0\). Apply once: \(\dfrac{e^x-1}{2x}\). Still \(0/0\). Apply again: \(\dfrac{e^x}{2}\to\dfrac{1}{2}\).

question.en: A 10-foot ladder rests against a vertical wall. If the bottom of the ladder slides away from the wall at a rate of 2 ft/sec, how fast is the top of the ladder sliding down the wall when the bottom is 6 feet from the wall?

solution.en:
Let \(x\) be the distance from the bottom of the ladder to the wall, and \(y\) be the height of the top of the ladder on the wall. By the Pythagorean theorem, \(x^2 + y^2 = 10^2 = 100\). When \(x = 6\), \(y = \sqrt{100 - 36} = 8\) ft.

Differentiate with respect to time \(t\):

\[ 2x\frac{dx}{dt} + 2y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \implies x\frac{dx}{dt} + y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0. \]

Substitute \(x = 6\), \(y = 8\), and \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 2\):

\[ 6(2) + 8\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \implies 12 + 8\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \implies \frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{12}{8} = -1.5\text{ ft/sec}. \]

The top of the ladder is sliding down at a rate of \(1.5\text{ ft/sec}\).
